content: Blindness is a condition characterized by the absence of visual perception, which can result from physiological or neurological causes. Various scales have been developed to measure the degree of vision loss and to define blindness. Total blindness refers to the complete inability to perceive form and light, clinically recorded as NLP, which stands for no light perception. The term blindness is often used to describe severe visual impairment, even when some residual vision remains. Individuals with only light perception can distinguish between light and dark but cannot perceive shapes or details. Those with light projection can identify the general direction of a light source. To determine who may require special assistance due to visual disabilities, different governmental jurisdictions have established more detailed definitions, often referred to as legal blindness. In North America and most of Europe, legal blindness is defined as having a visual acuity of 20/200 (6/60) or worse in the better eye, even with the best possible correction. This means that a legally blind person would need to be 20 feet (6 meters) away from an object to see it as clearly as a person with normal vision could from 200 feet (60 meters). Additionally, individuals with a visual field of less than 20 degrees (compared to the normal 180 degrees) are also classified as legally blind, even if their visual acuity is better than 20/200. Approximately 10% of individuals classified as legally blind have no vision at all. The remaining 90% retain some degree of vision, ranging from light perception to relatively good visual acuity. The term low vision is sometimes used to describe visual acuities between 20/70 and 20/200. According to the 10th Revision of the WHO International Statistical Classification of Diseases, Injuries, and Causes of Death, low vision is defined as a visual acuity of less than 6/18 but equal to or better than 3/60, or a corresponding visual field loss to less than 20 degrees in the better eye with the best possible correction. Blindness, by this classification, is defined as a visual acuity of less than 3/60 or a visual field loss to less than 10 degrees in the better eye with the best possible correction. Several organizations, such as the International Agency for the Prevention of Blindness, ORBIS International, and the Seva Foundation, have developed programs aimed at preventing blindness. In the United States, approximately 2 million people, most of whom are over the age of 65, are affected by blindness. Nutrients such as lutein and zeaxanthin have been shown to reduce the risk of age-related macular degeneration (AMD), as reported in the journal Archives of Ophthalmology. Foods rich in these nutrients include kale, turnip greens, collard greens, romaine lettuce, broccoli, zucchini, corn, garden peas, and Brussels sprouts.
